Records authorized for account administrators also stay unredacted when you export Redshift system table data to Amazon S3 Tables. You get precise, auditable control over who can see logs, and secure logging stays on. The feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Redshift is supported. To learn more, see federated permissions , Usage Notes and secure logging in the Amazon Redshift documentation.

title: AWS improves regional resiliency for root user sign-in
text: AWS root user sign-in is now served across US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon), with sign-in traffic distributed across all three Regions. This change reduces reliance on US East (N. Virginia) and improves resiliency during service disruptions. AWS automatically routes your root user sign-in to a supported Region without requiring you to select a Region or change how you sign in. This improvement is available now for all AWS accounts. In AWS CloudTrail, ConsoleLogin events for root user sign-ins are recorded in the Region that processed the sign-in request. To maintain full visibility into root user sign-in activity, update your monitoring and alerting to cover US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). To learn more, see the AWS Sign-In documentation and the CloudTrail ConsoleLogin event reference .

title: Amazon S3 Express One Zone is now available in 7 additional AWS Regions
text: The Amazon S3 Express One Zone storage class is now available in 7 additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Singapore), South America (Sao Paulo), US West (N. California), Canada (Central), Europe (Paris), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Seoul). Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single-Availability Zone storage class purpose-built to deliver consistent single-digit millisecond data access for your most frequently accessed data and latency-sensitive applications. S3 Express One Zone delivers data access speed up to 10x faster and request costs up to 80% lower than S3 Standard. It enables workloads such as machine learning training, interactive analytics, and key-value caching in AI search engines to achieve fast data access with high durability and availability. With this expansion, S3 Express One Zone is now available in 15 AWS Regions . For pricing details, visit the S3 pricing page . To learn more, visit the product page and documentation .

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio CI/CD adds notebook promotion and AI-assisted manifest generation
text: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio CI/CD expands its open-source deployment toolkit with two new capabilities: (1) an AI agent skill that automates manifest authoring, and (2) native notebook promotion across environments. Together, they help data teams go from project to production faster while maintaining best-practice defaults across stages. AI-assisted manifest generation. The new generate-bundle-manifest agent skill inspects a project's connections, storage, and workflows and produces a ready-to-use deployment manifest. It applies least-privilege IAM guidance, substitutes environment variables in place of hardcoded resource identifiers, and sets safe defaults such as opt-in catalog handling. Teams can import the skill into their own agents to standardize how they package and promote SageMaker Unified Studio projects across development, test, and production accounts. Native notebook promotion. The CI/CD toolkit now supports promoting native SMUS Notebooks alongside code, workflows, and catalog assets. Notebook promotion uses an in-place synchronization model that creates a notebook on first deployment and updates it on subsequent deployments, preserving run history across releases. Teams can promote every notebook in a project or select specific notebooks by ID, and a dry-run mode validates S3 connectivity, IAM permissions, and notebook counts before deployment. Notebook promotion integrates with the existing bundle, deploy, destroy, and dry-run commands and requires no changes to current pipeline structure. Both capabilities are open source and available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is offered. To get started, visit the CICD-for-SageMakerUnifiedStudio repository on GitHub. For more information, see the CI/CD for Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio documentation .

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports ODBC connections for Microsoft Power BI and other analytics tools
text: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports ODBC connections, so data users can connect Microsoft Power BI and other ODBC-compatible tools directly to governed data in SageMaker Unified Studio projects using the Amazon Athena ODBC driver. This adds a native connection path for analysts who have standardized on Power BI to work with governed data using their existing tools and workflows. Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio adds an ODBC connection details view to the project overview page, alongside the existing JDBC view. From the project's JDBC and ODBC connections tab, data users can copy the connection string and its parameters for a DSN-less connection, or use them to configure a named DSN. The Amazon Athena ODBC driver (version 2.2.0.1 or later) works directly with SageMaker Unified Studio through two modes: SageMakerBrowserIdc, which opens a browser to sign in through AWS IAM Identity Center and your external identity provider, and SageMakerIam, which uses temporary AWS credentials. ODBC connections in SageMaker Unified Studio are available today in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available, at no additional cost. To get started, refer to the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio User Guide and the Amazon Athena ODBC driver documentation .

title: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports model caching for faster inference autoscaling and reduced cold starts
text: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports model caching, an inference optimization that pre-loads model weights and container images onto cluster nodes so pods start in seconds instead of minutes. When running LLM inference at scale for workloads like chat assistants, agentic pipelines, RAG, and document analysis, cold start is a real bottleneck. Deployments and scale-out events spend most of their time downloading container images and model weights. As model size increases, this gets worse, with large models taking tens of minutes before they can serve traffic. Model caching solves this with two independent capabilities. The weights cache stores model weights on local NVMe so pods read from fast local storage instead of pulling from S3 or FSx over the network. The image cache pre-pulls the container image so pods skip the ECR download entirely. If a pod lands on a node without a warm cache, it falls back to pulling from the original source automatically, so there is no risk of pods getting stuck or failing. Benchmarks across models from 57 GB to 145 GB show around 60% faster scale-out, and the image cache cuts over two minutes of image-pull time (97% reduction). The benefit grows with model size while retaining the reliability of the original source path. Customers enable model caching through the HyperPod Inference Operator by adding a modelCacheConfig section to their InferenceEndpointConfig or JumpStartModel resource. The operator handles the full lifecycle with no manual setup or cleanup. Model caching is now generally available in all regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To get started, see the SageMaker HyperPod documentation .

title: AWS Systems Manager now diagnoses more issues that cause EC2 instances to be unmanaged
text: Today, AWS Systems Manager extends its diagnosis capability to identify six additional categories of issues that can prevent Amazon EC2 instances and hybrid-activated nodes from becoming managed by Systems Manager. An instance must be managed by Systems Manager before you can patch it, run commands, connect with Session Manager, or collect inventory, and when an instance is unmanaged the cause can be difficult to isolate. The diagnosis previously covered network connectivity, and it now also identifies issues with IAM permissions, SSM Agent version, instance status checks, operating system configuration, Default Host Management Configuration, and hybrid activation. With this broader coverage, more of your instances return a specific, actionable cause instead of an unidentified result, so you can bring your fleet under management faster. You run a diagnosis across your instances in the Systems Manager unified console experience, and Systems Manager reports the specific issues it finds in each category. Every diagnosed issue comes with step-by-step guidance to help you resolve it, and for some issues you can also run an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook from the console to remediate the issue directly. AWS Systems Manager diagnosis capability is available in all AWS Regions that are enabled by default. The capability runs as AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks, so you pay standard Automation usage charges for the runbooks you run; see AWS Systems Manager pricing for details. To learn more, see the AWS Systems Manager User Guide , or visit the AWS Systems Manager product page .

title: AWS Transfer Family SFTP Connectors now support continuing file transfers during credential rotation
text: AWS Transfer Family SFTP Connectors now continue running file transfers while you rotate the credentials used to authenticate with remote SFTP servers. You no longer need to update the connector to point to a new secret version each time a credential rotates, removing a manual step and helping avoid failed transfers during the rotation window. Connectors can now retrieve credentials from an ordered list of AWS Secrets Manager version stages, such as the current and previous versions, during authentication. The connector automatically tries each version in the order you specify and proceeds with the first that succeeds, so transfers continue uninterrupted as credentials are rotated on either side. You configure this when you create or update a connector, and the connector's credentials must be stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Support for continuing transfers during credential rotation is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transfer Family SFTP Connectors are supported. To learn more, visit the AWS Transfer Family User Guide . Get started with AWS Transfer Family in the AWS Transfer Family console .

title: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL announces Extended Support minor 12.22-rds.20251114 and 11.22-rds.20251114
text: Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) for PostgreSQL announces Amazon RDS Extended Support minor version 12.22-rds.20251114 and 11.22-rds.20251114. We recommend that you upgrade to this version to fix known security vulnerabilities and bugs in prior versions of PostgreSQL. Amazon RDS Extended Support provides you more time, up to three years, to upgrade to a new major version to help you meet your business requirements. During Extended Support, Amazon RDS will provide critical security and bug fixes for your PostgreSQL databases after the community ends support for a major version. You can run your PostgreSQL databases on Amazon RDS with Extended Support for up to three years beyond a major version’s end of standard support date. Learn more about Extended Support in the Amazon RDS User Guide . You can leverage automatic minor version upgrades to automatically upgrade your databases to more recent minor versions during scheduled maintenance windows. Learn more about upgrading your database instances, including automatic minor version upgrades, in the Amazon RDS User Guide . Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL makes it easy to set up, operate, and scale PostgreSQL deployments in the cloud. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL is available in all commercial and gov cloud region. See Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL for pricing details. Create or update a fully managed Amazon RDS database in the Amazon RDS Management Console .

title: AWS Certificate Manager now supports ACME issuance through AWS PrivateLink
text: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) now supports AWS PrivateLink for ACME public certificate issuance, allowing you to request and renew public TLS certificates over a private network path that stays within the AWS network. You can now create a VPC interface endpoint to the ACM ACME service and route issuance traffic from any ACMEv2-compatible client through your VPC. If you're already using ACME with ACM, setup requires no changes to your ACME clients. After you create your managed ACME endpoint in ACM, you create a standard VPC interface endpoint using the VPC console, AWS CLI, or AWS CloudFormation. Private DNS resolves your existing ACME directory URL to the interface endpoint inside your VPC automatically, so the same client configuration and directory URL continue to work with no reconfiguration. Issuance operations—account creation, order creation, domain validation, finalization, and certificate retrieval—then flow over PrivateLink. All activity remains visible in the ACM console with AWS CloudTrail logging and Amazon CloudWatch metrics for auditability. AWS PrivateLink support for ACME certificate issuance is available in all commercial AWS Regions. Standard AWS PrivateLink charges apply for interface endpoints; see the AWS PrivateLink pricing page. For ACM pricing details, see the ACM pricing page . To get started with ACME and PrivateLink, visit the AWS News blog post or read the documentation .

title: Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
text: Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory now prices short-term memory (STM) based on the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, replacing the previous flat rate per event. AgentCore memory gives agents in-session context through short-term memory and persistent knowledge across sessions through long-term memory. With consumption-based pricing, developers building agents that write frequent, small events pay in proportion to what they use. STM is priced across three dimensions: ingestion at $1.00 per GB, retrieval at $0.20 per GB, and storage at $0.10 per GB-month. Ingestion and retrieval are billed per event with a 12 KB minimum and 64 KB maximum billable size, while storage is billed on each event's actual size. Most workloads see lower costs, with small-payload use cases seeing the largest reductions. You can manage storage costs by setting a shorter time to live (TTL) on your memory resources. Long-term memory pricing is unchanged. Consumption-based pricing for AgentCore Memory short-term memory is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is offered. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing page .

title: Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS now support On-Demand Capacity Reservations
text: Starting today, you can reserve compute capacity for your Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS DB instances in one or more Availability Zones for as long as you need it. Reserving capacity helps ensure that DB instance create, restore, scale-compute, and start operations don't fail because of insufficient capacity. On-Demand Capacity Reservations are designed for workloads that need assurance that specific DB instance capacity will be available when they need it for business-critical events, such as migrations, product launches, seasonal peaks, high-availability deployments, or disaster recovery. You choose the DB instance class, engine, Availability Zones, and reserved capacity per Availability Zone, and RDS holds that capacity for you. Capacity can be reserved in two or more Availability Zones to support Multi-AZ deployments. To use the reserved capacity, reference the reservation when you create, restore, modify, or start a DB instance. You can reserve capacity for immediate use with no commitment and cancel at any time, or schedule a reservation to begin 5 to 120 days in the future with a minimum commitment. Reserved capacity is billed at On-Demand rates while the reservation is active, whether or not DB instances within the reservation are running. Discounts from your existing Reserved DB Instances or Database Savings Plans apply automatically. On-Demand Capacity Reservations are available for Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS in all AWS commercial Regions. To learn more about On-Demand Capacity Reservations, visit the documentation for Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS .

title: GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock
text: Amazon Bedrock now supports GLM 5.3 from Z.ai, giving you a powerful new option for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering work. Customers using GLM 5.3 on Amazon Bedrock have access to the latest open weight model with the AWS security and compliance posture. GLM 5.3 is Z.ai’s flagship model, a mixture-of-experts architecture with 753B total parameters and roughly 40B active per token, built on the same base model as GLM 5.2 with all improvements driven by scaled post-training. It combines a 1-million-token context window with up to 128K output tokens, and reasoning is always enabled with selectable effort levels so you can trade latency and token consumption against task performance. Bedrock support for GLM 5.3 includes explicit prompt caching with cache points on system prompts and messages, helping you reduce latency and input costs when reusing context across model calls. GLM 5.3 is available to eligible enterprise customers, and is accessible through the US and Global cross-Region inference profiles. To get started with GLM 5.3, you can access the model in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions , endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation . To learn more, read the launch blog post .

title: Amazon CloudWatch log centralization now available in AWS GovCloud and additional commercial Regions
text: Amazon CloudWatch log centralization is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) and 13 additional commercial Regions. CloudWatch log centralization copies log data from multiple AWS accounts and Regions into a single destination account, integrating with AWS Organizations for efficient aggregation without the need for custom solutions. With this launch, organizations in the AWS GovCloud (US) partition and commercial partition can each centralize logs across their accounts and Regions for centralized monitoring. You can scope centralization rules to your entire organization, specific organizational units, or selected accounts and copy logs into a single account while preserving source context through enriched system fields. CloudWatch log centralization is now additionally available in Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan), Europe (Spain), Europe (Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Middle East (Bahrain), Middle East (UAE), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). For a complete list of supported Regions, see the AWS Region table . To get started, create a centralization rule in the Amazon CloudWatch console, or by using the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, see Log centralization in the Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide. Customers can centralize one copy of logs for free; additional copies are charged at $0.05/GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing .

title: Amazon Connect Customer now provides automated checks to improve performance evaluation forms
text: Amazon Connect Customer now suggests changes to performance evaluation forms that improve the accuracy of evaluations automatically filled by AI. While setting up an evaluation form, managers can run an automated check that compares the form against best practices with a single click. Managers then receive a list of evaluation questions that are missing context for AI to score reliably, along with suggestions to make them more specific. For example, the check might flag "Did the agent provide a sales disclosure?" and prompt the manager to define exactly what the agent must disclose before a sale. This helps managers automatically score human and AI agents fairly and accurately, while spending less time refining their evaluation forms. This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, please visit our documentation and our webpage . For information about Amazon Connect Customer pricing, please visit our pricing page.

title: Amazon Corretto October 2026 Patch Updates
text: On October 26, 2026 Amazon announced a patch update for the following Amazon Corretto Long-Term Support (LTS) and Feature Release (FR) versions of OpenJDK. Corretto 27.0.1.0.11, 25.0.5.0.10, 21.0.13.0.11, 17.0.21.0.11, 11.0.33.0.10, and 8u512 are now available for download . Amazon Corretto is a no-cost, multi-platform, production-ready distribution of OpenJDK. Visit the Corretto home page to download Corretto 27, Corretto 25, Corretto 21, Corretto 17, Corretto 11, or Corretto 8. You can also get the updates on your Linux system by configuring a Corretto Apt, Yum, or Apk repo . Feedback is welcomed !

title: Amazon DynamoDB introduces filtered export to Amazon S3
text: Amazon DynamoDB now supports filtered export for tables. Export to Amazon S3 allows you to export your table data for analytics, data sharing, and other offline uses, as either a full export or an incremental export over a time window. Filtered export enables you to specify exactly which items and attributes to export, producing a dataset that contains only the data relevant to your use case. With filtered export, you use a key condition expression on a key attribute and a filter expression on any attribute to select which items to export, and a projection expression to choose which attributes to include. The export then returns only the items and attributes you want. You can use that subset of data to perform granular data recovery, move a slice of data between accounts, or run analytics while meeting your compliance rules. Filtered export works with both full exports and incremental exports. Filtered export is available in all AWS Regions, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, see the following resources: DynamoDB data export to Amazon S3 in the DynamoDB developer guide Filtering a table export in the DynamoDB developer guide Introducing filtered export from Amazon DynamoDB to Amazon S3 blog post

title: Amazon EC2 Hpc8a instances are now available in Asia Pacific (Singapore)
text: Starting today, Amazon EC2 Hpc8a instances are available in Asia Pacific (Singapore) region. These instances are powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors (formerly code named Turin). With a maximum frequency of 4.5GHz, Hpc8a instances deliver up to 40% higher performance and up to 25% better price performance compared to Hpc7a instances, helping customers accelerate compute-intensive workloads while optimizing costs. Compared to Hpc7a instances, Hpc8a instances also provide up to 42% higher memory bandwidth, further improving performance for memory-intensive simulations and scientific computing workloads. Built on the latest sixth-generation AWS Nitro Cards , Hpc8a instances are designed for compute-intensive, latency-sensitive HPC workloads. They are ideal for tightly coupled applications such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD), weather forecasting, explicit finite element analysis (FEA), and multiphysics simulations that require fast inter-node communication and consistent high performance. To get started, sign in to the AWS Management Console . For more information visit the Amazon EC2 Hpc8a instance page or AWS news blog .

title: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS)
text: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), enabling you to run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU. GPU sharing helps you increase GPU utilization and reduce infrastructure costs for workloads that use only part of a GPU's capacity, such as small-model inference, AV/ADAS simulations, embedding generation, and multi-model serving. With GPU sharing, you can pack more workloads onto each GPU instance without changing your application code. You define the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally set a maximum share of GPU compute, and Amazon ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale and deploy. GPU sharing is supported on Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. On Amazon ECS Managed Instances, Amazon ECS also monitors the MPS control daemon that enables sharing on each instance. If the daemon stops or becomes unhealthy, Amazon ECS automatically replaces the instance and moves your tasks to healthy capacity, so your GPU workloads keep running without manual intervention. To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, or other infrastructure-as-code tools to create a capacity provider with NVIDIA GPU instances, set the GPU sharing strategy and memory in the container definition of your task definition, and create a service on that capacity provider. This capability is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions . To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS GPU sharing documentation .

title: Amazon EKS Dashboard now provides fleet-wide visibility into certificate authority (CA) rotation
text: Today, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) announces certificate authority (CA) rotation visibility in the Amazon EKS Dashboard, giving you a consolidated view of CA rotation across your clusters. The Amazon EKS Dashboard already provides centralized visibility into your clusters across AWS Regions and accounts, and it now includes CA rotation, so you can see where action is needed without checking each cluster individually. Each Amazon EKS cluster has its own CA, and clusters created since 2018 have CAs with a 10-year validity period that are now approaching the point where rotation activities should begin. In the EKS Dashboard, you can now see your clusters and their CA rotation status, which clusters have CAs approaching expiration, and upcoming automated rotation events, so platform teams who operate many clusters can prioritize action across their fleet from one place. The Amazon EKS Dashboard aggregates data across your accounts and Regions through AWS Organizations, so you enable trusted access for the dashboard in your organization’s management account to use this capability. You view the dashboard from the US East region (us-east-1), and it is available at no additional cost. CA rotation support extends to all commercial AWS Regions, and the dashboard brings that rotation status together in one fleet-wide view. To learn more, see the Amazon EKS documentation .

title: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime
text: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration from self-managed Valkey and Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 with zero downtime. Zero downtime means zero Errors returned to the client during migration, measured the same way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. Your application continues reading and writing through cutover, and you do not need third-party replication tools. Online migration runs in three steps. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, and complete the cutover. ElastiCache gives you a migration endpoint your application can point to when you prepare the migration, and data replicates continuously from your source once you start the sync. You choose when writes move to the serverless cache, with a manual cutover or an automatic one once your data is in sync. ElastiCache records each step as an event on the cache’s Events tab, with the reason for any failed step. Online migration connects to your source using encryption in transit (TLS) and authentication, and reads credentials from AWS Secrets Manager, so your existing security controls stay in place. Online migration supports self-managed caches in cluster mode on Amazon EC2 running Redis OSS 4.0 through 7.2 or Valkey 7.2 through 8.1, and you can migrate them straight to Valkey 9.0. Migration usage is free for the first 180 days per AWS account, starting when the account first prepares a migration. After that, you pay per node-hour for the migration nodes that ElastiCache runs to replicate your data, for as long as a migration is active. The ElastiCache Serverless cache is billed separately at standard data storage and ECPU rates, including during the free period. For pricing details, see Amazon ElastiCache pricing . Online migration is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To get started, create or select an empty ElastiCache Serverless cache to migrate into, then start the migration from the ElastiCache console or the AWS CLI. To learn more, see the documentation .

title: Amazon EMR now supports native data quality checks in Apache Spark jobs
text: Amazon EMR now validates data quality natively within Apache Spark jobs. Data engineering teams can catch quality issues inline before bad data reaches downstream systems, without building or maintaining separate validation infrastructure. Amazon EMR Data Quality, powered by AWS Glue, is available at no additional cost and uses the same declarative rules language (Data Quality Definition Language) and APIs as AWS Glue for a consistent experience across both engines, and works with Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, and Delta Lake across EC2, EKS, and Serverless deployment modes. With this feature, you can author validation rules in your Spark scripts or reference rules stored in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and then apply them at any stage of your pipeline i.e., after reading data, during transformation, or after processing. With 30+ rule types, including dynamic rules that compare against historical runs and ML-based anomaly detection for tracking drift over time without specifying fixed thresholds, Amazon EMR Data Quality provides the flexibility of choosing the validation framework that fits your needs. You can take actions like failing a pipeline, filtering invalid records, or routing them to quarantine based on the quality evaluation results. Results are produced at the dataset, rule, and row level, so that you can easily identify which records or rules are driving the quality failures. Amazon EMR Data Quality is available on AWS runtime for Apache Spark (emr-spark-8.1.0) in all AWS Commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS China Regions. To get started, visit Amazon EMR Data Quality documentation and add DQDL rules for data quality validation to the Spark scripts of your EMR workloads.

title: Amazon GameLift Servers adds CPU burstability for container fleets
text: Amazon GameLift Servers now supports CPU burstability for container fleets, giving game developers greater flexibility in how compute resources are allocated and consumed at runtime. Previously, container fleets relied on a fixed CPU value that simultaneously controlled both container packing density and imposed a hard runtime cap. This dual constraint forced developers to choose between efficient resource utilization and maintaining performance headroom for their game server workloads. Game server workloads are inherently bursty, CPU demand stays low during most of a match but spikes sharply during physics calculations, AI processing, or collision detection. With CPU burstability, developers can now pack containers based on typical CPU needs while still allowing game server processes to burst into available idle instance CPU during peak demand moments. This opt-in feature is configured per container group definition, supports high-density deployments without sacrificing peak performance, and is included at no additional cost as part of standard container fleet pricing. CPU burstability for Amazon GameLift Servers container fleets is available in all AWS Regions where container fleets are supported, excluding China Regions. To learn more about CPU burstability for Amazon GameLift Servers container fleets, visit the Amazon GameLift Servers Developer Guide or explore the Amazon GameLift Servers product page .

title: Amazon MSK Connect and AWS Glue Schema Registry are now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region
text: Starting today, Amazon MSK Connect and the AWS Glue Schema Registry are available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. Together with Amazon MSK Standard brokers, already available in the region, these launches give customers running streaming workloads on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud a more complete set of tools to build, connect, and govern their Apache Kafka applications. MSK Connect lets you run fully managed Kafka Connect clusters with Amazon MSK - deploy, monitor, and scale connectors that move data between Apache Kafka and external systems like databases, file systems, and search indices, with no infrastructure to provision, automatic scaling, and pay-as-you-go pricing. Complementing it, the AWS Glue Schema Registry - a serverless, free feature of AWS Glue - lets you validate and control the evolution of streaming data using Apache Avro, JSON, and Protobuf schemas. Acting as a centralized repository for data format and structure across decoupled applications, it reduces data validation logic, cross-team coordination, and downstream failures, and integrates with C# and Java applications built for Amazon MSK , Amazon Kinesis Data Streams , Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink , and AWS Lambda . To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Developer Guide and the AWS Glue Schema Registry documentation.

title: Amazon MWAA now available in Mexico (Central) Region
text: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) Provisioned environments are now available in the Mexico (Central) Region (mx-central-1). Amazon MWAA Serverless was already available in this Region, and customers can now also use Amazon MWAA Provisioned environments for their Apache Airflow workflows. Amazon MWAA is a managed orchestration service for Apache Airflow that makes it easier for customers to set up and operate end-to-end data pipelines in the cloud at scale. Customers can create Amazon MWAA Provisioned environments using the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. Customers in Mexico (Central) can now run their Amazon MWAA Provisioned workflows closer to their data sources and end users, reducing latency and helping meet data residency requirements. To learn more, visit the Amazon MWAA product page and the Amazon MWAA supported Regions documentation .

title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports a 5-second default refresh interval
text: Starting today, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless reduces the default refresh interval to 5 seconds for both search and vector collections. The refresh interval controls how quickly newly ingested documents become available for search. By lowering the default from 10 seconds to 5 seconds, newly written data becomes searchable faster, giving applications quicker read-after-write visibility automatically, with no configuration changes and no action required on your part. This improvement applies to the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and takes effect by default on both search and vector collections. Faster refresh is valuable for workloads that continuously ingest data and need near real-time retrieval, including full-text search over frequently updated content as well as vector use cases such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, and recommendation and personalization systems. This means applications and AI agents can retrieve and act on the most recently ingested data sooner, improving the relevance and accuracy of search results and RAG responses for datasets that change frequently. The 5-second default refresh interval is available in all 24 regions where Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is available today. To learn more, see the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless documentation .

title: Amazon Quick Now Available in the AWS Singapore Region
text: Amazon Quick is now available in the AWS Asia Pacific (Singapore) region (ap-southeast-1). This launch allows customers in Singapore to access the full power of Amazon Quick while meeting local requirements for data sovereignty. Amazon Quick provides business users an agentic teammate that quickly answers questions at work and turns those answers into actions. With Amazon Quick, every user is empowered to make better decisions faster and take actions without switching applications using AI they can trust. Today’s launch allows customers to take advantage of Amazon Quick’s capabilities including AI-powered chat, Research, Spaces, and QuickSight dashboards — with their data stored and processed locally within the AWS Singapore region. For a full list of AWS regions where Amazon Quick is available, visit the Quick regional availability page. To learn more, visit the Amazon Quick documentation or product detail page .

title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports September 2026 Monthly Recommended Patch
text: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports the September 2026 Monthly Recommended Patch (MRP) for Oracle Database version 19c and 26ai. An MRP is a minor engine version that builds on a quarterly Release Update (RU), bundling Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) with additional Oracle-recommended fixes. The September 2026 MRP is applied on top of the July 2026 RU and includes the Oracle September CSPU . We recommend upgrading to the September 2026 MRP as it includes the latest security updates for Oracle Database. This release also includes the updated Oracle time zone file (DST version 46), which reflects the latest daylight saving time rule changes in several regions, including British Columbia and Alberta in Canada (effective November 1, 2026) and Morocco and Western Sahara (effective September 20, 2026), which are moving to permanent UTC offsets. If you store timestamps that include time zone information for these areas, the updated time zone file keeps that data aligned with the new rules. You can apply the September 2026 MRP for new database instances, or upgrade existing instances to engine version 19.0.0.0.ru-2026-07.mrp-2026-09.r2 or 26.0.0.0.ru-2026-07.mrp-2026-09.r2 from the Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. To learn more about Oracle MRPs supported on Amazon RDS for each engine version, see the Amazon RDS for Oracle Release notes .

title: Amazon S3 server access log delivery to Amazon CloudWatch Logs now available in five additional AWS Regions
text: Amazon S3 server access log delivery to Amazon CloudWatch Logs is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS China Regions. With your access logs in CloudWatch Logs, you can query them as they arrive, set alarms, and encrypt them with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys. This new delivery path complements the existing delivery of server access logs to S3 general purpose buckets, giving you more flexibility in how you monitor and analyze access to your data. With delivery to CloudWatch Logs, you can set alarms on error rates, monitor traffic patterns, investigate access incidents, and correlate S3 access activity with the rest of your operational data. S3 server access log delivery to CloudWatch Logs is now available in all AWS Regions. Amazon CloudWatch Logs charges for vended logs apply. For pricing details, visit Amazon CloudWatch pricing . To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 User Guide .

title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports serverless model customization for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8 and Ministral 3 models
text: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports serverless model customization for Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8 27B, and Ministral 3 3B, 8B, and 14B models. In addition to deploying these models on SageMaker AI, you can now adapt them to your specific domains and workflows, using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) techniques. You can also adapt these models with either low-rank adaptation (LoRA) or full fine-tuning techniques. This launch adds these models to a wide variety of models available for serverless customization on SageMaker AI, including models from the Nova, Gemma 4, Nemotron 3.5, Qwen, Llama, gpt-oss, and DeepSeek families. Model customization lets you tailor foundation models with your proprietary data so a smaller, right-sized model can match frontier-model quality on your tasks, while also reducing cost and latency. You can use labeled data with SFT to improve accuracy on domain-specific tasks, preference data with DPO to align outputs with your organization's tone, or reward signals with RFT to improve performance on new tasks. With serverless customization, SageMaker AI handles all infrastructure provisioning and training orchestration, so you can focus on your data and evaluation rather than cluster management, and only pay for what you use. Serverless model customization on SageMaker AI is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To get started, navigate to the Models page in Amazon SageMaker Studio to launch a customization job, use the SageMaker Python SDK or use our Agent skills with your choice of coding assistant. To learn more and see the full supported list of models, see the Amazon SageMaker AI model customization documentation .

title: Announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a managed ingress solution for your ECS services
text: AWS announces Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Gateway, a new resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized applications by dynamically provisioning and managing Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and their supporting resources directly in your account. With ECS Gateway, platform teams define organizational networking standards once on a gateway and associate it with one or more clusters, giving organizations a centralized way to govern how traffic reaches their ECS services. Application teams simply opt in to inherit those standards without requiring networking expertise. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing, allows up to 25 services to share an ALB to optimize infrastructure costs, and gives each service a unique Domain Name System (DNS) hostname. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs when capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. You can inspect these resources and the gateway route to each service to see exactly how requests reach your applications. For traffic and health monitoring, you can use standard ALB metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and target health information from Elastic Load Balancing. To get started, create an ECS Gateway, associate it with a cluster, and opt in your ECS service by adding the gateway connector parameter using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the awsvpc network mode across all launch types. It is available now in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when your services connect to the gateway. To learn more, refer to the AWS News blog and our documentation page.

title: AWS Lambda supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources
text: AWS Lambda now supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event source mappings (ESM), including Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. With this launch, customers can authenticate their Lambda Kafka consumers through their enterprise identity provider, helping them meet the security and compliance requirements for their Kafka applications. Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as payment processing, fraud detection, and real-time data pipelines use Kafka ESM to build serverless Kafka consumers. Kafka ESM provides automatic scaling, error handling, batching, and event filtering. Previously, Kafka ESM supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mutual TLS (mTLS) as authentication methods , so customers in regulated industries that require OAuth could not use Kafka ESM with their clusters. With OAuth support, customers can use their enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta, to authenticate their Kafka ESM and apply the same identity governance and access policies across their Kafka clusters and Lambda consumers. This capability is available in all AWS commercial Regions where self-managed Kafka ESM is available. To use OAuth authentication, create a new Kafka ESM with your authentication configuration through the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS SAM. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda developer guide and AWS Lambda pricing .

title: AWS announces TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch Support for AWS Trainium (Public Beta)
text: Today, AWS launched the public beta of TorchNeuron, an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium. Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed to deliver high performance and cost efficiency for deep learning AI training and inference workloads. TorchNeuron enables AI scientists and researchers to experiment and build models with PyTorch natively on Trainium. With TorchNeuron, developers can enable their PyTorch code on Trainium simply by switching to .to('neuron') while maintaining full PyTorch compatibility with eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. TorchNeuron is available as open source through the TorchNeuron github repo for Amazon EC2 Trainium2 instances and Amazon EC2 Trainium3 instances. To learn more about TorchNeuron and AWS Trainium accelerators, visit the AWS Neuron page .

title: AWS Backup adds restore testing support for Amazon Redshift
text: AWS Backup restore testing now supports Amazon Redshift. Restore testing helps you automate and periodically run restore tests of your backups, so you can confirm that your Amazon Redshift backups restore successfully and measure how long the restores take. You can now include Amazon Redshift in your restore testing plans alongside other supported AWS resources across storage, compute, and database services. Restore testing plans automatically select recovery points, run restores on a schedule, and measure restore job completion time against your recovery time objectives (RTO). This helps you evaluate recovery readiness and meet regulatory and compliance requirements for disaster recovery and business continuity. To get started, create a restore testing plan and assign your Amazon Redshift resources by Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or tag. Choose whether each test restores the latest or a random eligible recovery point. Optionally, use restore testing validation to confirm the restored resource before AWS Backup deletes the test resources. This support is available in all AWS Regions where both restore testing and Amazon Redshift are supported by AWS Backup. You can use the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. For a complete list of supported Regions and features, visit the AWS Backup documentation . To learn more about restore testing, visit the product page and pricing page .

title: AWS Batch now publishes job metrics to Amazon CloudWatch
text: AWS Batch now publishes job metrics to Amazon CloudWatch, providing native observability for batch workloads. AWS Batch emits metrics throughout the job lifecycle, giving you visibility into job queue health, failure rates, and job durations. AWS Batch automatically publishes job state transition and duration metrics to the AWS/Batch namespace in Amazon CloudWatch, with JobQueueName dimension. State transition metrics track how many jobs entered a given state, such as submitted, running, succeeded, or failed. Duration metrics track how long jobs spent between states, such as time from submission to runnable or total execution time. You can view these metrics in the AWS Batch console, the Amazon CloudWatch console, or through the AWS CLI and AWS SDKs. AWS Batch CloudWatch metrics are now published in all AWS Regions where AWS Batch is available. For more information, see CloudWatch Metrics page in the AWS Batch User Guide .

title: AWS Budgets now supports email verification for notification subscribers
text: AWS Budgets lets you set custom cost and usage thresholds and alerts you by email when your spending crosses the threshold. AWS Budgets now verifies new email subscribers before sending them budget alerts. When you add an email address to a budget notification, AWS Budgets sends a verification email to that address, and the address begins receiving notifications once the recipient confirms it. Verification applies to email addresses added from 9/30/26 onward. Addresses already subscribed on existing budgets are unaffected and need no action. For a new address, the recipient confirms it by following the link in the verification email, which opens the AWS Management Console. The AWS Budgets console shows the verification status of every subscriber, with a resend option for addresses still pending confirmation. AWS Budgets delivers these notifications through AWS User Notifications, and recipients can opt out at any time. AWS Budgets email verification is available in all AWS Regions, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see Adding email recipients to a budget notification in the AWS Billing and Cost Management User Guide.

title: AWS CloudFormation now simplifies stack update rollback operations
text: AWS CloudFormation now makes it simpler to complete an update rollback and get back to deploying. An update rollback returns your stack to a known good state. Starting today, if some resources cannot roll back automatically, force rollback enables you to complete the rollback in a single operation. It works across every CloudFormation workflow, from the AWS CLI , and SDKs to AWS CDK and AI agents. With force rollback, CloudFormation completes the update rollback and returns your stack to a deployable state in a single operation, instead of requiring you to identify, list, and retry the operation for each affected resource. Any resource that still needs attention, such as one affected by a change outside CloudFormation, is recorded for you to review and resolve it before your next deployment. To get started, run continue update rollback with the force rollback option, then create a drift-aware change set to review any configuration differences before your next deployment. To learn more, see Continue rolling back an update in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide. Force rollback is available in all Regions at no additional cost. Refer to the AWS Region table for service availability details.

title: AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now supports continuous penetration testing integrated directly into your CI/CD pipeline
text: AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing now integrates continuous penetration testing directly into your CI/CD pipeline (public preview) AWS Continuum for Penetration Testing (formerly AWS Security Agent) already provides continuous, on-demand penetration testing without the need to contract third-party pentest vendors. Now, in public preview, Continuum for Penetration Testing shifts security testing even further left by integrating directly into your existing CI/CD systems, making penetration testing a deploy-time event. Development teams ship code daily, but even with on-demand penetration testing available, security validation often happens outside the deployment workflow. CI/CD integration closes this gap. Developers receive findings, including severity, affected endpoints, and remediation guidance, directly in pipeline output. Non-security changes complete with no meaningful delay, and the pipeline automatically re-tests and verifies fixes after remediation without requiring manual re-triggers. Getting started requires no security expertise. An auto-generated pipeline snippet can be pasted into any existing pipeline and is completable in under five minutes. Application context bootstraps automatically on the first run, with no prior full penetration test required. Continuous penetration testing is available today. To get started, visit our documentation .

title: AWS Direct Connect announces 100G expansion in Manchester, England
text: Today, AWS announced the expansion of 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps dedicated connections with MACsec encryption capabilities at the existing AWS Direct Connect location in the Equinix MA3 data center near Manchester, England. You can now establish private, direct network access to all public AWS Regions (except those in China), AWS GovCloud Regions, and AWS Local Zones from this location. This is the third AWS Direct Connect location in England to provide 100 Gbps connections with MACsec encryption capabilities. The Direct Connect service enables you to establish a private, physical network connection between AWS and your data center, office, or colocation environment. These private connections can provide a more consistent network experience than those made over the public internet. For more information on the over 150 Direct Connect locations worldwide, visit the locations section of the Direct Connect product detail pages . Or, visit our getting started page to learn more about how to purchase and deploy Direct Connect.

title: AWS End User Messaging adds registration improvements for faster, higher-quality submissions
text: AWS End User Messaging now makes it easier to complete messaging registrations correctly the first time, with clearer guidance, explicit field requirements, and help avoiding the most common rejection reasons. Registrations ask for compliance evidence such as opt-in proof and sample messages, and submissions are often delayed or denied when that evidence is incomplete or a required field is missed. These improvements give you worked examples, surface exactly which fields you must provide, and walk you through the content that most often causes denials. First, example mock-ups of a compliant opt-in and sample messages are now included for US 10DLC, US short code, US toll-free and RCS registrations, so you can see what a compliant submission looks like before you build your own. Second, the registration API response now surfaces conditional logic, so you and your AI agents no longer have to guess which fields are required based on other field values. The response tells you which fields are required for your specific registration. Third, RCS registration now includes a walkthrough for recording the compliant video that agent registrations require. These improvements are available in all Regions where AWS End User Messaging registrations are available. To learn more and get started, see the End User Messaging User Guide .

title: AWS Health introduces the version catalog for software lifecycle management
text: Today, AWS Health introduces the version catalog which provides a centralized source of lifecycle information for software versions across AWS services. The version catalog helps customers move from reactive to proactive management of version upgrades and end-of-support risk. It is available in the AWS Health Dashboard, and customers on Business Support Plus, Enterprise Support, or Unified Operations can use the AWS Health API to integrate lifecycle data into their operational workflows. Customers running applications on AWS need to stay current with software versions to maintain a strong security and operational posture. AWS Health already sends account and resource-specific Planned Lifecycle Events well in advance for major version end-of-support milestones. The version catalog adds service-wide view of supported versions and their timelines, so customers can build upgrade schedules, governance controls, and move to newer supported versions before receiving an account-specific Planned Lifecycle Event. At launch, the version catalog covers multiple AWS services including Amazon RDS, Amazon EKS, and AWS Lambda with more services being added over time. The version catalog is available across all AWS Commercial Regions. To get started, visit the version catalog in the AWS Health Dashboard or read the documentation to learn more.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation
text: Trusted identity propagation carries a user's identity with their request, so AWS services can grant permissions based on who the user is and their underlying group associations, and log that user's access for auditing. With cross-Region support, this identity context can now be propagated to AWS services running in different AWS Regions, giving you greater flexibility in how you architect and deploy across AWS Regions. Customers often distribute workloads across AWS Regions for many reasons including separating the compute from the data it queries, to running workloads where capacity is available, or for disaster recovery and global scale. Previously, trusted identity propagation required all of the AWS services accessing a user's identity to reside in the same AWS Region. To reach services in another AWS Region, customers had to either grant access through broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users or consolidate all their services into a single AWS Region. With cross-Region trusted identity propagation, a user's identity travels with the request across AWS Regions automatically, so you can grant access based on who the user is and their underlying group associations, and audit who accessed which resources, while preserving fine-grained access control for every individual user. Cross-Region trusted identity propagation is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available. For the list of Regions where IAM Identity Center is available, see AWS Capabilities by Region. For more information, see Trusted identity propagation in the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports network access controls for Identity Store
text: AWS IAM Identity Center helps you configure the single sign-on experience for your workforce to AWS accounts and applications. IAM Identity Center now supports network access controls for Identity Store, which stores your users and groups. You can restrict access to the Identity Store API and the SCIM API based on the network that requests originate from. Your custom applications and user provisioning workflows use the Identity Store API to manage and look up users and groups, and your external identity provider uses the SCIM API to synchronize users and groups. For the Identity Store API, you can require that requests arrive only through allowed VPC endpoints in your account or organization, or from specific source VPCs. For both APIs, you can allow requests only from specific IP ranges. Within the same configuration, you can apply different restrictions to each API. For example, you can require that Identity Store API requests arrive only through VPC endpoints, while allowing SCIM requests from your external identity provider's published IP ranges. Network access controls are optional and turned off by default. Requests that AWS services make on your behalf are exempt. You configure network access controls by using the Identity Store API through the AWS SDKs and AWS CLI. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is offered. To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page . To get started with network access controls, see the Identity Store API Reference .

title: AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances
text: AWS Lambda now supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) for lazy loading Event Functions packaged as Open Container Initiative (OCI) images running on Lambda Managed Instances . With SOCI support, Lambda fetches only the files needed at each stage of the execution environment startup rather than downloading the entire image upfront, reducing container startup times by up to 70%. Customers building compute-intensive applications such as data processing pipelines, high-throughput API backends, and batch computation workloads require substantial memory and CPU resources to process large datasets, serve low-latency responses at scale, and run complex computations efficiently. Container images for these workloads can reach several gigabytes, and downloading and preparing the full image can take several minutes when provisioning new execution environments. SOCI support on Lambda Managed Instances eliminates this bottleneck by streaming only the required files at each stage of the execution environment startup, so your functions start faster as you scale. To get started, create a SOCI index (a table of contents for the files in your image layers) for your container image and push it to Amazon ECR . When creating or updating your function, set the image URI to the SOCI-indexed tag in Amazon ECR (for example, my-function:v1-soci) and publish a function version. Lambda automatically detects the SOCI index and enables lazy loading with no additional configuration. If you use a coding assistant such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex, install the Lambda Managed Instances skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS to configure and deploy functions through your agent. The feature is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Lambda Managed Instances is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Managed Instances developer guide .

title: The AWS MCP Server is now available in six additional AWS Regions
text: The AWS MCP Server is now available in six additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), and US West (Oregon). The AWS MCP Server, part of the Agent Toolkit for AWS , is a managed Model Context Protocol server that gives AI coding agents a single interface to AWS APIs, so agents can discover and call AWS services without building and maintaining per-service integrations. With this expansion, customers in these Regions can run the AWS MCP Server closer to their developers with lower latency, and keep request data within the Region to meet data residency requirements. For example, a development team in London can point its coding agents at a local endpoint to provision infrastructure, inspect running workloads, and debug failures without routing requests to another geography. The AWS MCP Server can access services in all commercial AWS Regions, while the AWS MCP Server itself runs in the Regions listed below. You can use AWS MCP Server in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), and Europe (London). To get started, see the following resources: - Getting started with the AWS MCP Server - AWS MCP Server endpoints and quotas

title: AWS Private CA now provides detailed certificate issuance logs
text: AWS Private CA announces detailed certificate issuance logs, a new AWS CloudTrail service event that records the complete certificate content, issuing CA information, requester identity, and signing status for every issuance. You can use these events for compliance auditing, certificate inventory, algorithm migration tracking, and failed-issuance monitoring. Previously, the CloudTrail management event for the IssueCertificate API confirmed that the API call succeeded by providing a certificate ARN but did not capture the certificate content, information about the CA that signed it, or issuances that failed before signing. The new IssueCertificateDetails event captures the complete to-be-signed (TBS) certificate with all X.509 fields and extensions, plus convenience fields for the subject, issuer, serial number, validity period, template, and signing algorithm. Events are emitted for both successful and failed issuance, so pre-signing failures such as name constraints violations now produce a record with a failure explanation. Each event identifies the requester: the account and IAM principal for direct API callers, or the service principal for certificates issued through AWS Private CA connectors or integrated AWS services. In cross-account configurations, the event is delivered to the CA owner account. The event is delivered automatically as a CloudTrail management event, with no configuration or opt-in required and no additional cost beyond standard AWS CloudTrail pricing. Because it flows through CloudTrail, you can act on it in real time with Amazon EventBridge or query it in batch with Amazon Athena for certificate auditing, inventory, tracking, and monitoring. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Private CA is offered. To learn more, see the AWS Private CA User Guide .

title: AWS Security Hub introduces remediation plans to prioritize and fix security exposures
text: AWS Security Hub now offers remediation plans that group related exposure findings sharing a root cause. Instead of addressing each exposure individually, you can now fix a single underlying resource, such as a misconfigured setting or overly permissive policy, and resolve or reduce the severity of multiple exposures at once. Each remediation plan includes prioritization guidance (Critical, High, Medium, or Low), impact assessment, and detailed step-by-step instructions with examples in multiple formats including AWS CLI, Terraform, CloudFormation, Python, and CDK. Security Hub automatically prioritizes plans so those reducing the most risk appear first, helping you focus remediation efforts where they matter most. AI agents can also programmatically consume remediation plans through the API to automate security fixes across your environment. Remediation plans are available in every AWS Region where AWS Security Hub is available and at no additional cost under AWS Security Hub Essentials plan. To learn more, visit the AWS Security Hub documentation .

title: AWS now lets customers sign up for AWS and pay invoices using ACH direct debit
text: Starting today, AWS customers in the United States can use a US bank account to sign up for AWS and pay for their AWS services through ACH direct debit. This feature provides a convenient and secure way to manage AWS payments directly from a USD bank account. Customers can securely connect a personal or business US bank account and use it to pay AWS invoices. Previously, new AWS customers needed a credit or debit card to complete signing up for an account. During sign-up, customers can choose Bank Account on the AWS sign-up page, select their bank, and authenticate using their bank's mobile app or online banking credentials. This securely verifies ownership and links their bank account to their AWS account. By default, the account will be used to pay future AWS invoices. Existing customers can add a bank account from the Payment preferences page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. They choose Add payment method, select Link your bank account, and follow the same bank-selection and authentication flow. Once verified, the bank account is available as a payment method to pay future AWS invoices.. ACH direct debit is available at no additional cost to AWS customers for USD bank accounts. To learn more, see Managing ACH direct debit .

title: AWS Transform for migrations expands support for existing landing zones
text: AWS Transform now supports more types of existing AWS environments when building landing zones for your migration, including AWS Control Tower landing zones and landing zones built with AWS Organizations. AWS Transform runs a foundation gap analysis of your current environment against AWS best practices and expands your landing zone on top of what's already in your target accounts, so your team can start migrating sooner. AWS Transform also now supports an Infrastructure as Code (IaC)-only mode for building landing zones for your migration. In this mode, AWS Transform analyzes your organization, generates recommendations, and produces IaC tailored to your migration plan in AWS CDK, Terraform, or Landing Zone Accelerator (LZA) format. IaC-only mode is designed for organizations that prefer not to grant AWS Transform direct access to their management account. AWS Transform can now connect through a delegated administrator (DA) account instead. It also benefits customers who manage their own deployment pipeline and don't need the agent to deploy automatically. The AWS Transform for migrations landing zone agent automates landing zone design end to end, including foundation setup, organizational unit (OU) and account structure, service control policies (SCPs), and workload accounts aligned to your migration planning and waves. You can deploy directly or generate IaC for your own pipeline. These new capabilities are available in all target AWS Regions supported by AWS Transform for migrations . To learn more, please visit the AWS Transform User Guide .

title: AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now support 1:1 NAT
text: AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now provide managed one-to-one network address translation (NAT) directly on their attachments, through integration with Regional Private NAT Gateway. This enables customers to connect private networks that share the same IP address ranges without renumbering either network, deploying a NAT appliance, or writing return-traffic rules. Networks with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) blocks have long been unable to communicate, a common blocker during mergers and acquisitions, when connecting partner networks over AWS Site-to-Site VPN, in multicloud connectivity, and when independently provisioned VPCs need to interconnect. Using this capability, customers can define address-translation rules on a AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN attachment, specifying the private IP range each source CIDR translates to, across Amazon VPC, AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and SD-WAN appliances connected through Transit Gateway Connect. Both services apply translation automatically in both directions, with no separate return-traffic rule and no NAT appliance to deploy. AWS operates, scales, and manages the NAT capability as part of the attachment. For example, if a customer acquires a business and both VPCs use 10.0.0.0/16, they translate one VPC's addresses to a non-overlapping range on its attachment and connect the networks immediately. Customers set it up in minutes using the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation, and monitor translated traffic through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and Amazon EventBridge events. AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN offer 1:1 NAT through Regional Private NAT Gateway in all AWS commercial regions where they operate. For full pricing details, see Amazon VPC pricing . To learn more, see the AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN product pages, and the AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN documentation.

title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now supports Standard tier for contextual grounding checks
text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now offers a Standard tier for contextual grounding checks, which detect and filter hallucinations by checking whether a model response is grounded in your reference source and relevant to the user's query. The Standard tier is more robust than the Classic tier. It supports responses that include reasoning or conversational content, scores differently worded responses with the same meaning more consistently, and provides more comprehensive language support, matching the Standard tier for content filters and denied topics. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards for generative AI applications on any foundation model through the ApplyGuardrail API. Until now, contextual grounding checks applied strict grounding suited to summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. With the Standard tier, you can also apply contextual grounding checks to conversational applications and to responses that reason over the source. You choose the tier for each guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console or API. Existing guardrails keep the Classic tier until you change them. Pricing is the same for both tiers. To use the Standard tier, your guardrail must use cross-Region inference with a guardrail profile. The Standard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation on contextual grounding checks and safeguard tiers , or visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails product page .

title: Announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS for node bootstrapping
text: For blockchain node operators running Ethereum or Solana, AWS is announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS, an initiative that publishes pre-synced public blockchain node chain data in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) so you can bootstrap a node from a snapshot instead of peer-to-peer syncing from the network. These snapshots are hosted on Amazon S3 within AWS infrastructure, enabling customers running nodes on AWS benefit from reduced latency and optimized data transfer. Blockchain Snapshots on AWS republishes each network's authoritative snapshot in a format optimized for parallel extraction across multiple cores, reducing setup time, that an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance can use. Snapshots cover Ethereum and Solana, are available at no charge, and refresh on the same cadence as the upstream provider. Use them to add capacity to a remote procedure call (RPC) fleet, recover a failed node, or re-sync a corrupted database. You can use Blockchain Snapshots on AWS in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Ireland), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). Access requires an Amazon EC2 instance in the same Region with an Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint. To get started, visit the Blockchain Snapshots on AWS documentation to access setup instructions and download the latest snapshots.

title: Claude Haiku 5.5 is now available on AWS GovCloud (US)
text: AWS GovCloud (US) now offers Claude Haiku 5.5, the fastest and most efficient model in the Claude 5.5 family, built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it costs around 75% less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. Claude Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic's most capable Haiku yet, a significant step up from Haiku 4.5 across coding, tool use, computer use, and agents. It's also the first Haiku with effort controls, so teams can tune cost against intelligence for each task. Haiku 5.5 fits work where speed and cost matter most: real-time experiences like voice agents, live support, and in-app assistants, and high-volume tasks like classification, summarization, and pulling key fields from documents. It's also a fast, cost-efficient subagent. A more capable model like Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand off well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku, making it practical to run many agents in parallel. Amazon Bedrock gives you Haiku's capabilities while keeping your data within AWS infrastructure with regional data residency and provides access through a unified service with AWS-managed features like Guardrails and Knowledge Bases. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation and regional availability .

title: Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock
text: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models across both the bedrock-runtime and the bedrock-mantle endpoint. Whether you call Claude through boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application's data model. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation . Structured outputs is available where claude models are available. For more information check the regional availability details page.

title: Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers
text: Amazon CloudWatch now supports conditional log routing and chained parsers via pipelines, giving you more control over how log data is transformed and which CloudWatch log group it's sent to. CloudWatch pipelines is a fully managed service that ingests, transforms, and routes telemetry to CloudWatch without managing infrastructure. Log pipelines often carry a mix of event types that belong in different places, and individual events can nest one log format inside another. With conditional log routing, you define routes that send each event to a different CloudWatch log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so you can separate events by severity, source, or type and apply the right retention and access controls to each. With chained parsers, you can apply multiple parser processors in sequence, where later parsers consume fields produced by earlier ones. For example, you can parse a JSON envelope first, then apply a Grok parser to a field it extracts. Together, these capabilities let you structure diverse log formats and route them to the right log groups in a single pipeline. Conditional routing and chained parsers are available in all commercial AWS Regions where CloudWatch pipelines is generally available. You can configure these capabilities using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To get started, see the Amazon CloudWatch pipelines documentation .

title: Amazon Connect Customer now measures the outcomes that drive retention and revenue
text: Amazon Connect Customer now scores the outcome of your customer interactions. It shows whether the customer left satisfied, is at risk of churning, made a purchase, or resolved their need in self-service. You can now see whether an interaction worked, not just how efficiently it ran.
